How to answer

  • 1, 3 and 5 have written anchors. Choose 2 or 4 when the truth lies between two anchors.
  • Score what operates at national scale today, not what has been announced or piloted.
  • Choose DK if you don't know. It isn't scored, but two or more DKs in a pillar mark it as having insufficient evidence.
  • Add one fact or source for each answer. Scores without evidence are counted, but flagged.
  • The United States baseline is hidden while you answer, so it doesn't anchor your scores. You can switch it on in the sidebar.
Full guidance is in Instructions; the method is in ReadMe.

ReadMe

A 40-item self-assessment that shows how ready a country is to adopt AI at national scale, using India's digital public infrastructure (DPI) journey as the reference case.

What this tool is

It supports the session "Preparing a country for AI scale". The session explores DPI, trusted data ecosystems, identity and consent frameworks, compute, talent, regulatory readiness and public-private collaboration. Each participant scores their country before the session. The scores are then compared with a reference baseline (this build: United States) and pooled across the group.

The eight pillars

P1–P3 are the rails India built for DPI. P4–P6 are what AI adds on top. P7–P8 decide whether the whole system is trusted and used. Each pillar has five questions.

Anchored responses

Each question has written descriptions for scores 1, 3 and 5, and 2 and 4 sit between them. This way, two respondents who choose a 3 mean the same thing. DK (don't know) is allowed and is not scored. If a pillar has two or more DK answers, it is reported as having insufficient evidence.

How the United States baseline was assumed (suggestive)

  1. Evidence scan. Public material on each pillar, as of . For India, this is the material in the pre-reads (see References).
  2. Same anchors as respondents. Each item is scored 1–5 against the same written descriptions respondents use.
  3. Factored pillar scores. A pillar's baseline is the mean of its five item scores, computed at build time, so the two can never disagree.
  4. Scoring rules: score what operates at national scale today, not what has been announced; score the national picture, not the best state or sector; where a law exists but its obligations are not yet in force, score at most 3.
  5. Range. Each pillar has a plausible low–high range that shows how far a well-informed reviewer could reasonably move the score.

Evidence and assumptions by pillar

Baselines in this project

Each baseline is a file in config/baselines/. The same questions are compared against whichever country you choose at build time.

Baselines are suggestive, not definitive. They are expert judgements, not survey results or official positions, and they go out of date as policies and infrastructure change. Use them as reference points to argue with, not verdicts. Facilitators can adjust them for each assessment, for example by updating the evidence, using an expert panel's median scores, narrowing the scope to a state or sector, or setting target scores instead of a peer country. Each baseline is a file in config/baselines/, and the project README explains how to change it.

How scores are computed

  • Pillar score = mean of non-DK items (blank if two or more items are DK).
  • Overall score = mean of the eight pillar scores.
  • Gap = your score − United States baseline.
  • Group score = median across respondents. Spread = interquartile range (Q3 − Q1). A spread above 1.0 marks a pillar where respondents disagree.

Your data

Everything runs in your browser. Answers are saved only in this browser's local storage, and nothing is sent to any server. To share results, export a JSON or CSV file from the Results tab. To clear your answers, use Reset my answers on the Start tab.

Customising and contributing

Questions, baseline scores, references and author details all live in JSON config files. Edit them and rebuild to make your own version. The source is in the project repository.

Instructions

For a single respondent it takes about 25 minutes. For a facilitated group, plan about a week before the session to collect responses.

For respondents

  1. Read the core pre-reads. The six starred items in References take about six hours.
  2. Fill in your profile on the Start tab: your name, organisation, the country you're assessing, your role and your familiarity with India's DPI.
  3. Answer each question on the Assess tab.
    • Read the three descriptions and pick the score that best matches the evidence you know.
    • Choose 2 or 4 when the truth lies between two descriptions.
    • Score what operates at national scale today, not what has been announced or piloted.
    • Choose DK if you don't know, rather than guessing.
    • Add one fact, source or example in the evidence box.
  4. Leave the United States baseline off while you answer, so it doesn't sway your scores. Switch it on afterwards to compare.
  5. Review your results on the Results tab: overall score, band, binding constraint, gaps and the questions to bring to the session.
  6. Export your response as JSON and send the file to the facilitator. Your progress is saved in this browser, so you can stop and come back.

For facilitators

  1. Share this file (or its hosted link) with participants one to two weeks before the session, with the core pre-reads.
  2. Collect the JSON exports. Ask everyone to name their file after themselves.
  3. Load all files on the Group tab by dropping them in together.
  4. Start with contested pillars. Where the spread is above 1.0, compare the evidence people gave before debating priorities.
  5. Agree the binding constraint. Use the lowest-scoring pillar and the largest gap to the United States baseline as starting points.
  6. Close with a first move. Agree one action, an owner and a 12-month marker for the weakest pillar.
  7. Export the group CSV for the session record.

Reading the results

Tips

  • Use Print / PDF on the Results tab to save a one-page record.
  • The theme button (◐) switches between light and dark mode.
  • To start again, use Reset my answers on the Start tab.
